It's a good question. Net Neutrality says you can't favor or block specific services. Let's say you don't have unlimited on TMO but are on a capped plan.

TMO treats the speed of all traffic the same. The difference is that it's not counting music/video against your cap. I guess where it's questionable is that it's favoring music/video services. As far as I know, they aren't taking in any money from companies to be whitelisted for this and it's supposedly relatively easy to get whitelisted. TMO isn't violating the spirit of the law but technically they're in violation.

For something like this, the FCC would need to re-write parts of the law or someone would have to bring on a lawsuit for the FCC to act. I don't think that companies like Comcast/Verizon/etc want the FCC to revisit the law because it could become 'worse' for them.

I guess you could argue that. I checked the rules again and you're correct that paragraph 18 "No Paid Prioritization" only forbids traffic shaping in exchange for compensation, which T-Mobile is presumably avoiding because it's not receiving any third party compensation for offering this feature; however, there is this bit in paragraph 20 "No Unreasonable Interference or Unreasonable Disadvantage to Consumers or Edge Providers"

The key insight of the virtuous cycle is that broadband providers have both the incentive and the ability to act as gatekeepers standing between edge providers and consumers. As gatekeepers, they can block access altogether; they can target competitors, including competitors to their own video services; and they can extract unfair tolls. Such conduct would, as the Commission concluded in 2010, “reduce the rate of innovation at the edge and, in turn, the likely rate of improvements to network infrastructure.”23 In other words, when a broadband provider acts as a gatekeeper, it actually chokes consumer demand for the very broadband product it can supply.

I would argue that forcing some traffic to count against your bandwidth cap and allowing other traffic not to count against your bandwidth cap could be considered an unfair toll to the provider whose services count to the limit. It's certainly a case of T-Mobile acting as a gatekeeper in which services impact your cap. It's a shakier argument than the paid prioritization argument, but as you correctly point out, T-Mobile's prioritizing isn't being compensated by a third party.
